a_not_b: Gambel oak has rounded lobes of even depth, and the sinuses cut a little more than halfway to the midrib.
b_not_a: Bur oak has its deepest pair of sinuses near the middle of the blade, cutting nearly to the midrib, so the leaf looks fiddle-shaped.
ref: FNA vol. 3, Quercus gambelii (taxon 233501032) and Quercus macrocarpa (taxon 233501058)

a_not_b: Silver maple has deep narrow sinuses, coarse teeth on the lobe margins, and a silvery white underside.
b_not_a: Sugar maple has shallow rounded sinuses, a smooth margin between the lobes, and a pale green underside.
ref: Virginia Tech Dendrology fact sheets 5, Acer saccharinum, and 2, Acer saccharum

a_not_b: Sugar maple has 5 rounded lobes and a smooth margin between the lobe tips.
b_not_a: Norway maple has 5 to 7 lobes with long pointed teeth, and a cut petiole leaks milky white sap.
ref: Virginia Tech Dendrology fact sheets 2, Acer saccharum, and 6, Acer platanoides

a_not_b: Silver maple has 5 sinuses that cut deep toward the petiole, and the underside is silvery white.
b_not_a: Norway maple has 5 to 7 broad lobes with long pointed teeth, and the underside is only a paler green.
ref: Virginia Tech Dendrology fact sheets 5, Acer saccharinum, and 6, Acer platanoides

a_not_b: Bigtooth maple has 3 blunt lobes with a few widely spaced rounded teeth, on a small blade about as wide as long.
b_not_a: Sugar maple has 5 lobes on a longer blade, and the margin between the lobes carries no teeth.
ref: Virginia Tech Dendrology fact sheets 587, Acer grandidentatum, and 2, Acer saccharum

a_not_b: Rocky Mountain maple has 3 to 5 sharply toothed lobes, and some leaves split into 3 separate leaflets.
b_not_a: Bigtooth maple has 3 to 5 blunt lobes with only a few widely spaced rounded teeth, and the blade stays in one piece.
ref: Virginia Tech Dendrology fact sheets 161, Acer glabrum, and 587, Acer grandidentatum

a_not_b: American sycamore sets its leaves one at a time along the twig, and the swollen petiole base hides the bud.
b_not_a: Norway maple sets its leaves in pairs, across from each other on the twig.
ref: Virginia Tech Dendrology fact sheets 36, Platanus occidentalis, and 6, Acer platanoides

a_not_b: Northern red oak has sinuses that cut a third to halfway to the midvein, and the underside is smooth.
b_not_a: Black oak has deeper sinuses, and the underside carries scruffy hairs with tufts in the vein angles.
ref: Virginia Tech Dendrology fact sheets 38, Quercus rubra, and 39, Quercus velutina

a_not_b: Northern red oak has wide flat-topped gray ridges with shallow furrows between them, in a pattern like ski tracks.
b_not_a: Black oak has thick, nearly black bark, deeply furrowed up and down with horizontal breaks, over a yellow-orange inner bark.
ref: Virginia Tech Dendrology fact sheets 38, Quercus rubra, and 39, Quercus velutina

a_not_b: Northern red oak has sinuses that cut less than halfway to the midrib, and the upper surface is dull green.
b_not_a: Shumard's oak has sinuses that cut more than halfway to the midrib, a glossy upper surface, and large hair tufts in the vein angles below.
ref: FNA vol. 3, Quercus rubra (taxon 233501079) and Quercus shumardii (taxon 233501082); Virginia Tech Dendrology fact sheet 169, Quercus shumardii

a_not_b: Shumard's oak has a long blade, 100 to 200 mm, broadly elliptic to obovate in outline.
b_not_a: Texas red oak has a shorter blade, 55 to 100 mm, and the outline is nearly circular.
ref: FNA vol. 3, Quercus shumardii (taxon 233501082) and Quercus buckleyi (taxon 233501014)

a_not_b: Pin oak has deep U-shaped sinuses that cut nearly to the midrib, so little blade is left between the lobes.
b_not_a: Northern red oak has sinuses that cut only a third to halfway to the midvein, so the blade looks solid and even.
ref: Virginia Tech Dendrology fact sheets 74, Quercus palustris, and 38, Quercus rubra

a_not_b: Pin oak has thin, tight, gray-brown bark, and dead down-pointing branchlets stay on the lower trunk.
b_not_a: Northern red oak has a clear lower trunk, and the bark breaks into wide flat-topped ridges with shallow furrows.
ref: Virginia Tech Dendrology fact sheets 74, Quercus palustris, and 38, Quercus rubra

a_not_b: White oak has 7 to 10 rounded finger-like lobes, and no deep waist across the middle of the blade.
b_not_a: Bur oak has two middle sinuses that nearly reach the midrib, and the lobes near the tip spread into a crown.
ref: Virginia Tech Dendrology fact sheets 35, Quercus alba, and 72, Quercus macrocarpa

a_not_b: White oak has whitish to ashy gray bark that breaks into irregular plates and blocks.
b_not_a: Bur oak has darker gray-brown bark, scaly but cut by clear vertical ridges on a large trunk.
ref: Virginia Tech Dendrology fact sheets 35, Quercus alba, and 72, Quercus macrocarpa

a_not_b: White oak has 7 to 10 narrow rounded lobes along an oblong blade.
b_not_a: Post oak has 5 lobes, and the two middle lobes are square, so the blade makes a cross.
ref: Virginia Tech Dendrology fact sheets 35, Quercus alba, and 77, Quercus stellata

a_not_b: Bur oak has a cup that covers at least half the nut, and soft awns on the rim make a fringe around it.
b_not_a: Post oak has a shallower saucer-shaped cup with flat tight scales, and the rim carries no fringe.
ref: FNA vol. 3, Quercus macrocarpa (taxon 233501058) and Quercus stellata (taxon 233501087)

a_not_b: Blackjack oak has 3 shallow bristle-tipped lobes at the wide end of a thick blade, so the leaf looks like a bell.
b_not_a: Black oak has 5 to 7 deeper bristle-tipped lobes and a more even outline.
ref: Virginia Tech Dendrology fact sheets 168, Quercus marilandica, and 39, Quercus velutina

a_not_b: Gambel oak has deep rounded lobes, with sinuses that cut more than halfway to the midrib.
b_not_a: Havard oak has a wavy margin with only 2 or 3 rounded teeth on each side, on a thick blade with a gray woolly underside.
ref: FNA vol. 3, Quercus gambelii (taxon 233501032) and Quercus havardii (taxon 233501042)
